Physics-Embedded Feature Learning for AI in
Medical Imaging
Pulock Das1, Al Amin2, Kamrul Hasan1, Rohan Thompson2, Azubike D. Okpalaeze2, Liang Hong1
1Tennessee State University, Nashville, TN, USA
2Huston–Tillotson University, Austin, TX, USA
Email:{pdas, mhasan1, lhong}@tnstate.edu,{aamin, rrthompson, adokpalaeze}@htu.edu
Abstract—Deep learning (DL) models have achieved strong
performance in an intelligence healthcare setting, yet most exist-
ing approaches operate as black boxes and ignore the physical
processes that govern tumor growth, limiting interpretability,
robustness, and clinical trust. To address this limitation, we pro-
pose PhysNet, a physics-embedded DL framework that integrates
tumor growth dynamics directly into the feature learning process
of a convolutional neural network (CNN). Unlike conventional
physics-informed methods that impose physical constraints only
at the output level, PhysNet embeds a reaction diffusion model
of tumor growth within intermediate feature representations of a
ResNet backbone. The architecture jointly performs multi-class
tumor classification while learning a latent tumor density field, its
temporal evolution, and biologically meaningful physical parame-
ters, including tumor diffusion and growth rates, through end-to-
end training. This design is necessary because purely data-driven
models, even when highly accurate or ensemble-based, cannot
guarantee physically consistent predictions or provide insight
into tumor behavior. Experimental results on a large brain MRI
dataset demonstrate that PhysNet outperforms multiple state-of-
the-art DL baselines, including MobileNetV2, VGG16, VGG19,
and ensemble models, achieving superior classification accuracy
and F1-score. In addition to improved performance, PhysNet
produces interpretable latent representations and learned bio-
physical parameters that align with established medical knowl-
edge, highlighting physics-embedded representation learning as
a practical pathway toward more trustworthy and clinically
meaningful medical AI systems.
Index Terms—Physics-embedded learning, reaction–diffusion
models, interpretable deep learning, medical image analysis
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning (DL) has become a dominant approach in
healthcare industries, especially for medical image analysis,
achieving remarkable success in tasks such as disease detec-
tion, classification, and segmentation [1], [2]. These advances
have created optimism for deploying artificial intelligence (AI)
systems in clinical decision support and diagnostic workflows.
Despite their strong predictive performance, most existing DL
architectures function as black boxes [3], [4]. They learn
complex patterns directly from data without considering the
underlying physical or biological processes that govern tumor
development and progression [5]. As a result, their predic-
tions lack interpretability, physical consistency, and clinical
transparency. In high-stakes medical applications, this limi-
tation raises concerns regarding robustness, trustworthiness,
and generalization, particularly when models encounter data
distributions that differ from their training set.Tumor growth is not an arbitrary process but fol-
lows well-established biophysical principles that describe
how cancer cells diffuse, proliferate, and interact with
surrounding tissue. Reaction-diffusion models, such as
the Fisher–Kolmogorov–Petrovsky–Piskunov (KPP) equation,
have long been used to characterize tumor expansion dynamics
in computational oncology [6], [7]. However, these physics-
based models are typically studied independently from modern
DL systems and are rarely integrated into data-driven image
classification frameworks.
Recent research on physics-informed deep learning (PIDL)
attempts to bridge this gap by incorporating physical con-
straints into neural networks. Most existing approaches, how-
ever, apply physics losses only at the network output level,
treating physical consistency as a post hoc regularization rather
than a core component of representation learning [8], [9]. As
a result, physics has a limited influence on the learned feature
space, and interpretability remains restricted.
To address these challenges, the following key contributions
are made:
•A physics embedded DL framework, termed PhysNet, is
introduced to integrate tumor growth dynamics directly
into the feature learning process of a CNN, rather than
enforcing physical constraints only at the output level.
•A dual branch architecture is developed to jointly perform
multi-class brain tumor classification and latent tumor
density evolution, enabling the learning of biologically
meaningful tumor behavior alongside accurate predic-
tions.
•A reaction diffusion tumor growth model with learnable
physical parameters is incorporated into intermediate
feature representations of a ResNet backbone, allow-
ing physical principles to guide representation learning
through end to end optimization.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion II reviews related work on DL for medical imaging,
physics-based tumor modeling, and physics-informed neural
networks. Section III presents the PhysNet framework, includ-
ing problem formulation, physics-based tumor growth model-
ing, architecture design, and training algorithms. Section IV
provides experimental results. Finally, Section V concludes the
paper and discusses future research directions.arXiv:2603.28057v1  [cs.LG]  30 Mar 2026

II. RELATEDWORK
A. Deep Learning for Brain Tumor Analysis
DL based methods have been widely applied to brain tumor
analysis using MRI, achieving strong performance in classi-
fication, segmentation, and detection tasks [10]–[12]. DNNs
such as VGG, ResNet, and MobileNet variants have demon-
strated high accuracy by learning hierarchical image features
directly from data [13]. More recent studies have explored
ensemble learning strategies to further improve robustness and
predictive performance [14], [15]. While these approaches are
effective in terms of accuracy, they remain purely data-driven
and offer limited interpretability, as they do not incorporate
domain knowledge related to tumor growth mechanisms.
B. Physics-Based Tumor Growth Modeling
Physics-based tumor growth models have been extensively
studied in computational oncology to describe the spatial and
temporal evolution of cancer cells [16]. Reaction diffusion
models, including the Fisher Kolmogorov Petrovsky Piskunov
equation, are commonly used to model tumor cell proliferation
and diffusion within biological tissue [17], [18]. These mod-
els provide strong biological interpretability and theoretical
grounding, but typically rely on handcrafted parameters and
are not designed for image based classification tasks. As a
result, they are often studied separately from modern DL
frameworks.
C. Physics-Informed Deep Learning
Physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) aims to combine
data-driven learning with physical consistency by embedding
governing equations into neural network training [19]. Most
existing physics-informed neural networks enforce physical
laws through additional loss terms evaluated at the network
output or at selected collocation points. While this strategy
improves physical consistency, physics is treated as a regular-
ization constraint rather than an integral part of feature learn-
ing. Consequently, physical principles have limited influence
on intermediate representations, and interpretability remains
constrained.

F . Training Algorithm
PhysNet is trained end-to-end by jointly optimizing classi-
fication performance and physical consistency. For each input
MRI image, two augmented views are generated. Geometric
transformations are shared across views to preserve spatial
correspondence, while photometric transformations are applied
independently. The two views are treated as a pseudo-temporal
pair for enforcing temporal consistency.
Both views are processed by a ResNet-50 backbone. Inter-
mediate feature maps (F 3) are used by the physics branch to
predict a latent tumor concentration fielduand its temporal
derivative∂u/∂t, while deeper feature maps (F 4) are used by
the classification branch to predict tumor class probabilities.
Physical parameters governing tumor growth, namely diffusion
coefficientD, growth rateρ, and carrying capacityK, are

learned jointly during training using positivity constrained
variables.
Training minimizes a multi-objective loss composed of
four terms: cross-entropy loss for classification, a physics
residual loss enforcing consistency with the Fisher–KPP reac-
tion–diffusion equation, a boundary smoothness loss promot-
ing biologically plausible tumor morphology, and a temporal
consistency loss linking the two augmented views. Gradients
from all loss components are backpropagated to update both
network parameters and physical parameters simultaneously.

IV. RESULTS ANDEXPERIMENTALANALYSIS
A. Dataset and Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted on a publicly available brain
MRI dataset comprising 3,264 T1-weighted images across
four classes: glioma (826 images), meningioma (822 images),
pituitary tumor (827 images), and no tumor (789 images).
Images were preprocessed to 224×224 resolution with inten-
sity normalization. The dataset was split 80/10/10 for training,
validation, and testing.
PhysNet was trained for 100 epochs using AdamW opti-
mizer (η= 2×10−4, weight decay10−4) with a cosine an-
nealing schedule. Loss weights were initialized asλ(0)
p= 0.01,
λb= 0.005,λ t= 0.01, with adaptive scheduling (Eq. 21,
α= 0.5). The Batch size was 32 with mixed-precision training
on NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Data augmentation included
random rotation (±15), horizontal flip (p=0.5), and color jitter.
B. Classification Performance
Figure 2 compares PhysNet against five baselines:
VGG16, VGG19, MobileNetV2, ResNet-50, and an ensemble
(VGG19+ResNet-50+MobileNetV2). PhysNet achieves 96.8%
accuracy and 96.2% F1-score, outperforming all baselines by

significant margins. Notably, PhysNet surpasses the ensemble
model (95.1% accuracy, 94.3% F1) despite being a single
architecture, demonstrating that physics-informed constraints
improve generalization beyond ensemble diversity. The perfor-
mance gain over vanilla ResNet-50 (94.2% accuracy) validates
that the physics branch provides complementary information
rather than merely adding parameters.
C. Physics-Embedded Feature Learning
Figure 3 visualizes the learned latent representations for
three tumor types. The concentration fieldu(x, t)exhibits
distinct spatial patterns: glioma shows diffuse boundaries (con-
sistent with infiltrative growth), meningioma displays compact
morphology (reflecting encapsulated nature), and pituitary
tumors demonstrate intermediate characteristics. The temporal
derivative∂u/∂tcaptures growth dynamics, with positive val-
ues concentrated at tumor cores indicating active proliferation.
Crucially, the Laplacian∇2ureveals physically inter-
pretable diffusion patterns. Negative values (blue) at tumor
centers indicate outward spreading, while boundary regions
show near-zero curvature satisfying the smoothness constraint
(Eq. 4). The PDE residual|R(x)|remains low across the
spatial domain (mean0.032±0.018), confirming that learned
features satisfy the Fisher-KPP equation within tolerance. This
demonstrates successful integration of physics constraints into
representation learning rather than post-hoc enforcement.
D. Learned Biophysical Parameters
Figure 4 presents the learned physical parameters across
tumor classes. Diffusion coefficients exhibit a clinically mean-
ingful ordering: glioma (D= 0.150±0.025mm2/day)>
meningioma (0.075±0.020)>pituitary (0.050±0.012),
consistent with known invasiveness. Proliferation rates follow
similar trends: glioma (ρ= 0.025±0.004day−1)>menin-
gioma (0.012±0.003)>pituitary (0.008±0.002), reflecting
aggressive growth kinetics of glioblastomas. Carrying capacity
Kvaries inversely with aggressiveness, suggesting spatial
constraints differ by tumor histology.
The correlation plot (Fig. 4, right) reveals a positive corre-
lation betweenDandρwithin glioma samples (Pearsonr=
0.72,p <0.001), indicating that rapidly proliferating tumors
also exhibit higher invasion rates—a hallmark of malignant
phenotypes. Meningioma and pituitary tumors show tighter
parameter clustering, reflecting more homogeneous biological

E. Training Dynamics and Ablation
Figure 5 illustrates multi-objective optimization behavior.
Classification lossL clsdominates initially (epoch 0–20), while
physics lossesL phys,Lboundary ,Ltemporal decrease more gradu-
ally, demonstrating complementary learning dynamics. Total
loss converges smoothly without oscillations, indicating stable
optimization despite competing objectives.Adaptive weightingλ pincreases from 0.01 to 0.087 over
training (Fig. 5, bottom-right), progressively enforcing physics
constraints as classification stabilizes. This automatic bal-
ancing eliminates manual hyperparameter tuning. Validation
accuracy tracks training accuracy closely (96.8% vs. 97.1% at
epoch 100), with minimal overfitting gap, suggesting physics
regularization improves generalization.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each component:
removing theL phys reduces accuracy to 94.8% (similar to
vanilla ResNet-50), removingL boundary yields noisy spatial
fields with unphysical discontinuities, and removingL temporal
increases residual magnitudes by 40%. Fixed weighting (λ p=
0.05constant) achieves only 95.3% accuracy, underperforming
adaptive scheduling by 1.5%, demonstrating the value of
dynamic balancing.
F . Computational Efficiency
PhysNet adds 1.2M parameters (2.1% increase) over
ResNet-50 baseline with minimal computational overhead:
2.91ms vs. 2.72ms per image (7% slower) on RTX 3090.
Training time increases from 45 to 52 minutes per epoch
due to Laplacian computation and multi-loss backpropagation.
Memory consumption rises from 3.2GB to 3.8GB per batch.
These modest costs are offset by interpretability gains and
improved accuracy, making PhysNet practical for clinical
deployment.

V. CONCLUSION ANDFUTUREWORK
This work introducedPhysNet, a physics-embedded deep
learning framework that integrates reaction–diffusion tumor
growth dynamics directly into CNN feature learning. Unlike
conventional physics-informed approaches that impose con-
straints only at the output level, PhysNet embeds the Fisher–
KPP equation within intermediate representations, allowing
physical priors to shape learned features. Although evaluated
on 2D MRI slices, the method directly extends to 3D vol-
umetric data. The proposed model achieves 96.8% accuracy
and a 96.2% F1-score, outperforming ensemble and state-of-
the-art baselines while simultaneously learning biologically
interpretable parameters (D,ρ,K) consistent with tumor
biology. In particular, learned diffusion coefficients correctly
rank tumor invasiveness (glioma>meningioma>pituitary),
and the inferred spatial fieldsu(x, t)exhibit histologically
consistent morphologies without explicit supervision. With
minimal computational overhead (7% inference time, 2.1%
additional parameters), PhysNet remains practical for clinical
deployment. Overall, embedding domain knowledge as differ-
entiable constraints improves both predictive performance and
interpretability in medical AI.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces PhysNet, a novel physics-embedded deep learning framework designed for AI in medical imaging, specifically for brain tumor classification. The main points covered are:

*   **Addressing Limitations of Black-Box DL Models:** Existing deep learning models in healthcare often act as "black boxes," lacking interpretability, robustness, and clinical trust because they ignore the underlying physical processes governing tumor growth.
*   **PhysNet's Core Innovation:** PhysNet integrates tumor growth dynamics directly into the feature learning process of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), unlike conventional physics-informed methods that apply constraints only at the output level.
*   **Architecture and Functionality:** PhysNet uses a ResNet backbone with a reaction-diffusion model of tumor growth embedded within its intermediate feature representations. This architecture jointly performs multi-class tumor classification and learns a latent tumor density field, its temporal evolution, and biologically meaningful physical parameters (diffusion and growth rates) through end-to-end training.
*   **Benefits of Physics Embedding:** By embedding physics, PhysNet aims to ensure physically consistent predictions, provide insights into tumor behavior, and enhance interpretability and trustworthiness, which are crucial for clinical applications.
*   **Experimental Validation:** The document highlights that PhysNet outperforms several state-of-the-art DL baselines on a large brain MRI dataset, achieving superior classification accuracy and F1-score.
*   **Key Contributions:** The paper emphasizes its contributions in introducing a physics-embedded framework, a dual-branch architecture for joint classification and latent evolution learning, and the incorporation of a reaction-diffusion model with learnable parameters into intermediate feature representations.

structure.title: RELATEDWORK
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses related work in brain tumor analysis and introduces a new methodology called PhysNet.

The "Related Work" section covers three main areas:
*   **Deep Learning for Brain Tumor Analysis:** This highlights the success of deep neural networks (DNNs) like VGG, ResNet, and MobileNet in brain tumor classification, segmentation, and detection using MRI data. However, it notes their limitation in interpretability due to their purely data-driven nature, lacking incorporation of domain knowledge about tumor growth.
*   **Physics-Based Tumor Growth Modeling:** This section describes traditional computational oncology approaches that use physics-based models, such as reaction-diffusion equations (like the Fisher-Kolmogorov Petrovsky Piskunov equation), to simulate tumor cell evolution. These models offer strong biological interpretability but are typically handcrafted and not designed for image-based tasks, leading to their separation from deep learning.
*   **Physics-Informed Deep Learning:** This introduces the concept of combining data-driven learning with physical consistency by embedding governing equations into neural network training. It points out that current methods often treat physics as a regularization constraint, limiting its influence on intermediate feature learning and interpretability.

The "Methodology" section then outlines the proposed **PhysNet framework**, which aims to integrate reaction-diffusion tumor growth dynamics directly into the feature learning process of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The methodology is broken down into:
*   **Problem Formulation:** It redefines the learning problem to jointly optimize classification performance and physical consistency, moving beyond purely data-driven classification.
*   **Physics-Based Tumor Growth Model:** It details the use of the Fisher-Kolmogorov Petrovsky Piskunov (Fisher-KPP) equation to model tumor cell density evolution, defining the parameters for diffusion, proliferation, and carrying capacity.

nodes.title: Physics-Based Tumor Growth Model
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses related work in brain tumor analysis and introduces a novel framework called PhysNet. The related work section covers:

*   **Deep Learning for Brain Tumor Analysis:** Highlights the success of deep learning (DL) methods like DNNs (VGG, ResNet, MobileNet) in classification, segmentation, and detection tasks using MRI data. However, it notes their lack of interpretability due to being purely data-driven.
*   **Physics-Based Tumor Growth Modeling:** Explains the use of physics-based models (e.g., reaction-diffusion equations like Fisher-Kolmogorov Petrovsky Piskunov) in computational oncology to describe tumor evolution. These models offer biological interpretability but are typically not designed for image-based tasks and are studied separately from DL.
*   **Physics-Informed Deep Learning (PIDL):** Describes PIDL as an approach that combines data-driven learning with physical consistency by embedding governing equations into neural network training, often through additional loss terms. It points out that in existing PIDL methods, physics acts as a regularization constraint rather than an integral part of feature learning, limiting its influence on intermediate representations and interpretability.

The document then transitions to its **Methodology**, outlining the proposed PhysNet framework. Key aspects of the methodology include:

*   **Problem Formulation:** Reformulates the learning problem to jointly optimize classification performance and physical consistency, aiming to learn a classifier, a latent spatial field representing tumor cell density, and physical parameters governing tumor growth.
*   **Physics-Based Tumor Growth Model:** Adopts the Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (Fisher-KPP) reaction-diffusion equation to model tumor cell density evolution, incorporating diffusion, logistic growth, and carrying capacity. It also defines boundary conditions to ensure physically realistic tumor morphology by enforcing smoothness constraints.
*   **PhysNet Architecture Design:** Details the PhysNet architecture, which is based on a ResNet-50 backbone and includes novel components:
    *   **Latent Field Prediction Heads:** Predicts latent fields for tumor concentration and its temporal evolution from intermediate ResNet features.
    *   **Learnable Physical Parameters:** Learns diffusion coefficient (D), proliferation rate (ρ), and carrying capacity (K) during training, providing interpretable insights.
    *   **Physics-Informed Loss Integration:** Embeds physics directly into the feature learning process through specialized loss functions.
*   **Physics-Embedded Feature Learning:** Explains how physical consistency is enforced at the feature level. This involves:
    *   **Physics Loss Formulation:** Penalizing violations of the reaction-diffusion equation using a mean squared residual on a discrete spatial grid.
    *   **Boundary Smoothness Loss:** Penalizing high curvature at tumor boundaries to promote biologically plausible shapes.
    *   **Temporal Consistency Loss:** Introducing pseudo-time consistency using data augmentation to provide temporal supervision without explicit time labels.

nodes.title: PhysNet Architecture Design
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the boundary conditions and architecture of a model called PhysNet, designed for tumor morphology analysis.

**Main points covered:**

*   **Boundary Conditions:** Smoothness constraints are applied to tumor boundaries using the Laplacian of the tumor field being approximately zero ($\nabla^2 u(x, t) \approx 0$). This penalizes high curvature and promotes biologically plausible tumor shapes.
*   **PhysNet Architecture:**
    *   It uses a **ResNet-50 backbone** pre-trained on ImageNet for feature extraction.
    *   It incorporates three novel components:
        *   **Latent field prediction heads:** These predict two latent fields, $u(x)$ (tumor concentration) and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x)$ (temporal evolution), from intermediate features of the ResNet backbone (specifically, layer 3). These are learned latent quantities, not direct observations.
        *   **Learnable physical parameters:** Instead of fixed values, physical parameters like diffusion ($D$), reaction rate ($\rho$), and carrying capacity ($K$) are learned during training using softplus activation to ensure positivity.
        *   **Physics-informed loss integration:** Physical consistency is embedded at the feature level, not just the output.
*   **Physics-Embedded Feature Learning:**
    *   **Physics Loss Formulation:** A physics loss ($L_{physics}$) is defined based on the residual of the reaction-diffusion equation, penalizing deviations from the governing PDE. The Laplacian is approximated using a finite difference scheme.
    *   **Boundary Smoothness Loss:** A boundary loss ($L_{boundary}$) penalizes high curvature at the tumor boundary, identified by thresholding the gradient magnitude of the predicted tumor field.
    *   **Temporal Consistency Loss:** A pseudo-time consistency loss is introduced using data augmentation. Two augmented views of an input image are treated as observations at different pseudo-times, and a relationship is enforced between the predicted temporal derivative and the difference in predicted fields.

nodes.title: Physics-Embedded Feature Learning
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the PhysNet framework, a novel approach for tumor morphology analysis that integrates physics-informed learning into a deep neural network. The main points covered are:

*   **Boundary Conditions:** Smoothness constraints are imposed on tumor boundaries using a Laplacian approximation to ensure biologically plausible morphology.
*   **PhysNet Architecture:** The network is built on a ResNet-50 backbone and includes three key novel components:
    *   **Latent Field Prediction Heads:** These heads predict a latent tumor concentration field (`u`) and its temporal evolution (`∂u/∂t`) from intermediate ResNet features.
    *   **Learnable Physical Parameters:** Instead of fixed values, physical parameters like diffusion coefficient (`D`), growth rate (`ρ`), and carrying capacity (`K`) are learned during training, providing interpretability.
    *   **Physics-Informed Loss Integration:** Physical consistency is enforced at the intermediate feature level, not just the output.
*   **Physics-Embedded Feature Learning:** The core innovation is embedding physics within the feature representation. This is achieved through:
    *   **Physics Loss:** Penalizing violations of the reaction-diffusion equation by calculating the mean squared residual.
    *   **Boundary Smoothness Loss:** Penalizing high curvature at tumor boundaries to promote realistic shapes.
    *   **Temporal Consistency Loss:** Using data augmentation to create pseudo-temporal pairs and enforce consistency between predicted temporal evolution and actual changes.
*   **Multi-Objective Optimization:** The total training objective combines classification accuracy with physics-based losses (physics, boundary, and temporal) using adaptive weighting to balance these competing objectives.
*   **Training Algorithm:** PhysNet is trained end-to-end by jointly optimizing classification and physical consistency, utilizing augmented views of MRI images as pseudo-temporal pairs.

nodes.title: Multi-Objective Optimization
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the PhysNet framework, a novel approach for tumor classification that integrates a deep learning model with physics-based constraints. The main points covered are:

*   **PhysNet Architecture:** It utilizes a ResNet-50 backbone for feature extraction. A key innovation is a "physics-embedded branch" that enforces reaction-diffusion tumor growth dynamics at an intermediate feature level, aiming for physically consistent and interpretable representations.
*   **Loss Function:** The training objective is multi-objective, combining classification accuracy (`L_cls`) with physical consistency (`L_physics`, `L_boundary`, `L_temporal`).
*   **Adaptive Weight Scheduling:** To manage the trade-off between objectives, an exponential moving average (EMA)-based adaptive weighting scheme is employed. This allows the model to prioritize classification initially and gradually incorporate physics constraints as classification performance improves.
*   **Training Algorithm:** PhysNet is trained end-to-end. The process involves generating two augmented views of each input MRI image, applying shared geometric transformations and independent photometric transformations. These views are treated as a pseudo-temporal pair to enforce temporal consistency.
*   **Feature Usage:** Intermediate feature maps (F3) are used by the physics branch to predict tumor concentration and its temporal derivative, while deeper feature maps (F4) are used by the classification branch for predicting tumor class probabilities.
*   **Physical Parameters:** The framework aims to learn physical parameters governing tumor growth, such as diffusion coefficient (D), growth rate (ρ), and carrying capacity (K).

nodes.title: Training Algorithm
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes the PhysNet framework, a deep learning model for tumor classification that integrates physics-informed constraints. The main points covered are:

*   **PhysNet Architecture:** It uses a ResNet-50 backbone for feature extraction and a physics-embedded branch that enforces reaction-diffusion tumor growth dynamics at an intermediate feature level.
*   **Multi-Objective Optimization:** The training objective combines classification accuracy with physical consistency, including terms for classification loss, physics residual loss, boundary smoothness loss, and temporal consistency loss.
*   **Adaptive Weight Scheduling:** An exponential moving average (EMA)-based adaptive weighting scheme is used to balance the competing objectives during training, allowing the model to prioritize classification initially and then progressively enforce physics constraints.
*   **Training Algorithm:** PhysNet is trained end-to-end by jointly optimizing classification and physical consistency. It involves generating augmented views of MRI images, processing them through the backbone, predicting latent tumor fields and their derivatives, and learning physical parameters (diffusion coefficient, growth rate, carrying capacity) simultaneously.
*   **Dataset and Experimental Setup:** Experiments were conducted on a brain MRI dataset with four classes, and the model was trained using specific hyperparameters and data augmentation techniques.
*   **Classification Performance:** PhysNet achieved superior classification accuracy and F1-score compared to several baseline models, including an ensemble, demonstrating the benefit of physics-informed constraints.
*   **Physics-Embedded Feature Learning:** Visualizations show that the learned latent representations (tumor concentration, temporal derivative, Laplacian) exhibit distinct spatial patterns consistent with tumor biology and adhere to physical constraints.
*   **Learned Biophysical Parameters:** The model successfully learned biologically plausible physical parameters (diffusion coefficient, proliferation rate, carrying capacity) that align with known tumor invasiveness and growth kinetics, without explicit supervision.
*   **Training Dynamics and Ablation Studies:** Analysis of training dynamics shows complementary learning of different loss components and the effectiveness of adaptive weighting. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each loss component for optimal performance.
*   **Computational Efficiency:** PhysNet introduces a modest increase in parameters and computational overhead, making it practical for clinical deployment.
*   **Conclusion:** PhysNet effectively integrates reaction-diffusion tumor growth dynamics into deep learning feature learning, leading to improved performance and interpretability in medical AI.
